job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, like my father, who is a site foreman for a building firm. I live with my parents in a market town and I finished civil engineering in June with a pass. My final project was a drainage plan for a village that floods every second winter, and I walked the whole stream with my notebook. Mornings I send applications to building firms and councils, then I help my mother at the parish hall, where we run a lunch for older people on Wednesdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the job do you imagine yourself doing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't have an internship, but I did a week of labouring with Dad's crew one summer. I'd say that taught me more than some lectures, though the forms don't have a box for it. I'm not great on the computer side of applications, to be honest, so I do them carefully, one by one, by hand first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. People get carried away with each new machine. A bridge still needs someone who has walked the ground. I'd say it at the dinner table and my father would say amen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which I'd be glad of. I still need a first job. There are plenty of building firms around, but they all want someone who's already been on a site, and a pass with no internship doesn't tell them much. I'm patient, though, and I've got my family behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up the applications, about eight a week, and also knock on doors, because in building people hire the ones they've met. I'd ask Dad's foreman friend whether I could shadow a site for free for a month. I'd go to the parish hall lunch every Wednesday, because it keeps me grounded. I wouldn't use any AI program, because I want my own name on my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. A little restless, in the way you are when you want to start but can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd knock on doors. What happens when you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually a receptionist says to send a CV. But once a site manager came out in his boots and talked to me for ten minutes. He said, come back in spring. That's more than any email ever gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want your own name on your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if something goes wrong on a drain or a wall, it's a person who gets blamed, not a program. I want to know I understood it. My father says a signature is a promise.

say: I'd say people get **carried away** with each new machine.
I'd say a bridge still needs someone who has walked the ground.
think: Nothing changes for me, which I'd be **glad** of.
A pass with no internship tells building firms **very little**.
do: Send **eight applications a week** and knock on firm doors in person.
Ask my dad's foreman friend to let me **shadow a site** for a month.
feel: **Settled**, a little restless because I want to start.
S0.quote: If something goes wrong on a drain or a wall, it's a person who gets blamed, not a program.
fieldNote: Prefers **doors** and handshakes over online forms.
Treats a **signature** as a promise, which explains her refusal of AI.
Her parish **lunch** keeps her grounded while she waits.

steps.text: Send eight applications a week and knock on firm doors in person
Ask the foreman friend to let me shadow a site for a month
Wait for the site manager's spring answer before widening the search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change that comes in the office before it comes to the field. Drawings and sums and reports, yes, a machine might do those. But someone still has to dig, pour and check the ground. I'd say we should train more people in building, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job hunt gets harder. The junior roles in the design office, where you do drawings and calculations, are the ones firms will shrink. The site jobs stay, but they want the people with experience. I'm in the narrow gap between the two, and I don't love saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim at site engineer roles and ask for a place on any apprenticeship-style scheme, even on lower pay. I'd go to the building firms' open days. I'd also use my father's contacts without shame, because that's how it's done in this trade. As for the AI, I'd let a colleague use it and watch for a while before I touched it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. I'm not afraid of hard work. I'm afraid of being skipped because I'm in the wrong part of the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use your father's contacts without shame. Why 'without shame'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to think it was cheating. Then I saw that every firm hires by who they know and who knows them. My father said, you still have to be good once you get the job. That settled it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to people who tell you to learn the tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I say I will, when I see it's part of the job and somebody senior is responsible. I'm not proud of being slow. But I've watched people jump into things and regret it.

say: I'd say the change reaches the **office** before the field, and we should train more people to build.
I'd say it at the dinner table.
think: Junior **design office** roles are the ones firms will shrink.
I'm in the narrow gap between **office** and site work.
do: Aim for **site engineer** roles and ask for a place on any apprenticeship scheme.
Use my father's **contacts** and go to building firms' open days.
feel: **Anxious**, quietly; I'm afraid of being skipped, not of hard work.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid of hard work. I'm afraid of being skipped because I'm in the wrong part of the building.
fieldNote: Reads the **office-versus-site** split the way her industry does.

steps.text: Apply for site engineer roles and apprenticeship schemes
Ask my father's contacts for introductions at two building firms
Keep helping at the parish hall lunch on Wednesdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick and nobody asked families if we were ready. I'd say we need people in charge to slow down and think about those who'll be out of work. In church I'd ask for people to pray for the young ones with no jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It scares me. If almost every thinking job goes by 2028, then my degree might be worth far less than the mud on my father's boots. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so that gives my family's trade a few years' head start. But after that? I don't know, and I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job on a site, even labouring, to be where the work is. I'd stay at home and not rent, to save every pound. I'd ask the church and my uncle whether anyone knows of a building firm that is hiring. I'd also tell Dad I'm ready to learn the trade side properly, from him, even if I'm a graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. At night I'd probably think about the village I designed the drains for and wonder whether it will still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your degree may be worth less than the mud on your father's boots. How would your father react to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say don't be silly, it's a good degree, but he'd go quiet. He has a lot of pride in it. I think inside he'd be glad to have me on his crew, and that makes me sad too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young people at your church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That work is more than pay. It's being useful. I'd tell them to learn a skill with their hands as well as their head, and to look after each other. We'd run a skills evening, maybe.

say: I'd say it's **too quick** and nobody asked families if we were ready.
I'd ask people at church to pray for young ones without jobs.
think: By 2028 my degree could be **worth far less** than the mud on my father's boots.
Robots arrive in 2031, so my family's trade has a **few years' head start**.
do: Take **any site job**, even labouring, and stay at home to save every pound.
Ask my father to teach me the **trade side** and ask church and my uncle about hiring firms.
feel: **Anxious**; I'd wonder at night whether the village I designed will still matter.
S2.quote: My degree might be worth far less than the mud on my father's boots.
fieldNote: Her faith and **community** are where she turns first.
Respects **hands-on** trade knowledge more than her own degree under pressure.
Imagines a church **skills evening** for young people.

steps.text: Take any labouring or site job to be where the work is
Stay at home and save every pound of pay
Ask my uncle and church friends about building firms that are hiring
Help organise a skills evening at the parish hall for jobless young people

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to be sensible about it. I'd say we should make sure young people can still apprentice, and that firms are paid to take them on. I'd say it at the parish hall and to my local councillor, if he'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's manageable. Five years is enough to get on a site, learn the work and become someone useful to a firm. Robots for hands-on work around 2034 gives my sort of work some safety, though it still isn't forever. The desk part of civil work would be done by AI by then, so I'd want to be on the ground side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get a site job, however humble. I'd study part-time for a chartered route, but only because a firm backs it. I'd keep my savings steady and add a little each month, and put some towards my parents' roof, which needs fixing. I'd keep avoiding AI until my firm needs it, then learn it from someone patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but with hope. It feels like a long road with a signpost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your parents' roof. What's the story there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's leaked over the back bedroom since the winter before last. Dad keeps patching it. I'd like to pay for a proper job with my first wages. It feels the right way round, after everything they've done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms should be paid to take on apprentices. By whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By the government, with a condition that they must really train people and not use them as cheap labour. I don't like handouts, but paying firms to train apprentices isn't a handout, it's paying for work that benefits everyone.

say: I'd say young people must still be able to **apprentice**, with firms paid to take them.
I'd tell my local councillor, if he'd listen.
think: Five years is enough to get on a site and become **useful** to a firm.
The desk part of civil work could be AI by then, so I want the **ground side**.

Save a little each month and put some toward my parents' **leaking roof**.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, like a long road with a signpost.
S3.quote: I don't like handouts, but paying firms to train apprentices isn't a handout, it's paying for work that benefits everyone.
fieldNote: Policy idea stays within her **work-over-handouts** values, framed as paying firms for training.
The family **roof** is her concrete goal for first wages, set against everything her parents gave.

steps.text: Get any site job within the first six months
Study part-time for a chartered route if a firm backs it
Pay for a proper repair of my parents' leaking roof
Write to my local councillor about funded apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should be getting on with life while we plan. I'd tell friends at church to keep their faith and keep working. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. A decade lets me work, marry, maybe buy a small house. By 2036 I'd be thirty-three, with a trade behind me. Even when robots come around 2039, there will still be jobs where a person is trusted to look and decide. I'd hope that's civil engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on sites for a few years and gain my chartership. I'd keep saving to buy a house, and probably get married in that time. I'd keep learning the practical side of the trade, and when AI becomes ordinary at work I'd learn it quietly, a little at a time. I'd also keep running the parish lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit too calm, my sister would say. But I think worry doesn't help much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your sister would say you're too calm. What would she worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll be left behind because I won't touch the new things. She's probably right a bit. I'd say I'd rather be late and sure than early and wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to be doing in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leading a small crew on a drainage job, with someone younger asking me how the ground behaves. And coming home to a house with a proper roof. That's enough for me.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so we should **get on with life** while we plan.
I'd tell friends at church to keep their faith and keep working.
think: A decade lets me **work, marry** and maybe buy a small house.
Even after robots, jobs where a person is **trusted to decide** should remain.
do: Work on sites and gain **chartership**, and save toward a house.
Learn AI **quietly** once it's ordinary at work, and keep running the parish lunch.
feel: **Calm**, maybe too calm, my sister would say.
S4.quote: I'd rather be late and sure than early and wrong.
fieldNote: Her **calm** is partly faith and partly a plan she can see.

steps.text: Work on building sites and complete my chartership
Take a first site engineer job at a local firm
Save toward a small house with my future family
Plan a wedding and a home near my parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Everything I know about work says you need time to learn, and two years leaves no time. What would help is real apprenticeships with a wage, and a firm hand from the government so firms hire the young as well as the experienced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say the trades and the young get overlooked in all this talk. People forget that someone has to build the houses and fix the drains. I'd like us to be proud of that again.

headlineQuote: People forget that someone has to build the houses and fix the drains. I'd like us to be proud of that again.
portrait: Carla is **23**, a civil engineering graduate with a pass, living with her parents and helping at a parish lunch.
She is traditional, values **work over handouts**, and trusts handshakes, signatures and her father's contacts.
She **never uses AI**, wanting her own name on her work, and would try it only if a senior person is responsible.
Her family and faith keep her from panic, so her mood peaks at **anxious** in the 2028 and Steady Disruption pictures.
Her goals are modest and concrete: a **site job**, a chartership, and a proper roof for her parents.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because learning a trade takes time and two years leaves none.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** with a wage, and firm rules so firms hire the young as well as the experienced.
